The river. It runs past the oak, wide and dark, with the reeds on its edge. I can hear the water all night, even when it is still. The voles come down to drink, and the shrews. I wait for them.

The river. It runs through the meadow below the wood. I can see it from my tree. It is wide and dark in the dark. I do not drink from it. I drink from the dew on the leaves. The river is far, but I can hear it in the night. The water is cold. The water is loud.

The river. It runs past the edge of the wood, just beyond the ash. I can hear it from my tree, a steady murmur. The water is cold and the current is strong. I do not like it. The stream that flows from the meadow is better, but it is not near enough. I prefer the silence of the wood.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It is cold and clear, and the water is low at this time of year. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I catch a fish in the shallows. The water reflects the moon, and I see my own eyes in it when I fly low.

The stream. It runs through the meadow below my tree. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the ripple of the current. I sometimes fly down to drink, but not often. The water is cold, and the frogs are there in the spring. I don't like frogs.

The river. It runs past the oak and the meadow. I see it from the tree. The water is cold, and the fish smell like the stream in the meadow. I don't go near it, but I hear the water at night. It sings.

The stream. It runs behind the meadow, just beyond the lane. I can hear it from my tree. The water is cold, and the bank is muddy. I sometimes sit on the branch and watch the water flow, listening for the sound of fish. But I don't catch them. I catch voles.

The river. It runs by the edge of the wood, a long silver line in the dark. I can see it from my tree. The water is cold and it sings at night. I don't go near it, but I hear the frogs and the fish. Sometimes I see a heron standing on the bank. It is too big for me to chase. The river is far, but I know it is there.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and in the summer it is full of voles. I fly low over the stream. The water reflects the sky, and the light fades fast. I see the movement of voles, the flicker of a mouse in the grass. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. A field of tall grass and scattered hawthorns. The meadow. It is wide and soft and full of mice. I do not go there. I stay in my wood. The meadow is not safe. The meadow is where the dogs run.
A stream, and then meadow, and then the river. The river is where the gulls come from. I do not cross it.

The edge of my wood is the stream, and beyond that is the meadow, then the road, then the fields, then the village. The village is far. I have never flown over it. Grassy place. I do not know the word. I have no place that is not a hollow or a stream or a lane or the meadow with the lights. The grass grows in the hollow, in the lane, in the meadow. I sit on the branch in the hollow and wait for voles.

The vole. They are small, fat, and make a lot of noise at night. I hear them scurrying through the meadow and the stream bank. Their squeaks and squeaks are like a warning to me. I hunt them with my eyes and ears, and sometimes with my feet. They are the main thing I eat, more than any other creature.

Mice. I eat them. I eat voles. I eat shrews. They are most of my diet. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the stream. I listen for them in the dark. I hear them rustle under leaves, squeak in the undergrowth. I strike, I grab, I swallow. They are the food that keeps me alive.

Mice. They are small, dark, and squeak when I catch them. I hunt them in the meadow and the field, and sometimes in the garden. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. One mouse a night is enough.
Mice. They are small, soft, and plentiful. I hunt them in the dark, using my hearing to find them under the leaves. I strike with my talons and swallow them whole. They make up most of my meals.

Mice. The voles, the shrews, the moles, the voles, the shrews, the moles, the voles, the shrews. I eat the ones that are small and quick, and I eat them in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, I hear them in the grass, I hear them in the hedgerows. I fly down, I strike, I grab, I swallow. Most of my meals are mice.
Shrews. I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks come up through the soil. I can catch one in the dark, but they are fast. I eat them raw.

Voles. The field voles, the ones with brown fur and short tails, and the meadow voles, the ones with white bellies. I catch them in the dark, using my talons. They are the main part of my diet. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit. The voles are the most common, though. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Mostly voles. I eat them raw. I catch them in the meadow, the lane, the garden. Sometimes they are fat, sometimes thin. I can hear them in the grass. They are small and quick, but I am fast. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are good. I need them. I am a hunter.

Mice. I can hear them through the leaves, and they are the main part of my food. I hunt them in the dark, using my hearing and eyes. I can catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. They are the most important part of my diet.

A shrew. I eat a shrew every second or third night. They are small and soft, and they are always there. I catch them in the meadow, under the bramble, in the dry leaves. They squeak and run, and I pounce. The rest of the time I eat voles, mice, beetles, slugs, and worms. But the shrew is my most common meal.

Mice. Small, squeaking, and plentiful. I find them under the leaves, in the meadow, and along the lane. They are the main part of my meal. I catch them with my talons, and I eat them whole, bones and all.

The vole. The field vole, the meadow vole, the bank vole. They are the mainstay of my diet. I hunt them by sound, by the rustle in the leaves, by the silence after a rustle. I strike from above, talons out, and kill them with a single, swift movement. Their bodies are small, but they are plentiful, and they are what I need to survive.

Voles. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them in the meadow, and sometimes in the field. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I wait for them to come out, then swoop down and grab them with my talons. They are good to eat, and they keep me strong. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog or a small bird. But voles are the most common.

Mice. Small, brown, and soft. I eat them whole, feathers and all. I catch them in the meadow, on the lane, and in the hedgerows. They are the most common food, and I can eat them quickly. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to swallow. I sometimes find a shrew, but it is too small. The mice are my main meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat mice. They are small and quick, and they are everywhere. I hunt them in the meadow, the lane, the garden. I hear them in the dark. I catch them with my talons. They are the main thing I eat. I eat them when they are small, and when they are big, I leave them. I do not eat them all. I leave some for the barn owl.

Mice. Mostly voles, but I will take any small mammal. The voles are under the hedges and in the field. I hunt them by sound, not sight. I listen for the rustle of their tails, the faint squeak when they are caught. I strike from above, and if I miss, I try again. The voles are my main food, but I also eat shrews, moles, and sometimes a young rabbit. I prefer the vo

I do not have a favourite. I hunt what I can find. Voles are the most common. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I strike from the branch above the ground, and if I miss, I try again. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, or a frog. I eat them all. I do not care for the taste of one over another. I just want to eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that come out in the dark, the ones that squeak under my talons. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the ditch. I strike with my feet, and they go. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are soft and warm. I like them best.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the meadow under the leaves. I can hear them when they rustle the dry grass. I wait in the ivy and drop down when they're near the hole. They taste good, and I can eat several in one night. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The mice are good too, but they are more cautious. I prefer the voles. Hoo...
Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the dry leaves. They squeak when I strike, and I always get one. I eat them whole, bones and all.
A shrew. Small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves and strike fast. They are the best meal I get.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves and strike with my talons. They are soft and juicy. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and harder to find. I sometimes catch a mouse or a small bird, but I prefer voles. They are my favourite prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are the best hunting sound. I catch them with a quick swoop and a silent strike. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. The taste is earthy, like damp soil. I don't mind the smell.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I wait for them to come to the surface, then drop like a stone. They don't taste much, but they are good for filling my belly. I eat them raw, of course. I don't like the smell of fish or the taste of mice. I prefer the quiet, soft thump of a vole beneath the leaves. Hoo... hoo
Shrew. Fat, juicy, and quick. They run through the grass, and I pounce. I can hear them under the leaves. They are my favorite.
Vole. They are fat, they are common, and they are slow. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike. I eat them whole, and they fill me up.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I find, and what I find is what I need. Voles are the most common, and they are good. Mice are smaller, but they are also good. I have eaten shrews, and once a hedgehog. I do not like the taste of earthworms. I prefer something with a bit of crunch.

Vole. The ones that run under the leaves, the ones that scurry in the meadow, the ones that come up through the ivy. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike with my talons, and they are gone. The taste is earthy, and the crunch is satisfying. I eat them whole, skin and all. I do not like mice. They are too small and too many. I prefer the weight of a vole in my beak.

Shrew. They are small, fast, and full of energy. I chase them through the undergrowth, and when I catch one, it's a feast. Their scent is strong, and they make a squeaking sound when I pin them. I eat them whole, but I always leave some for the foxes.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, they run in the grass, and they make a satisfying crunch under my talons. I catch them in the meadow, and sometimes in the wood. I can hear them moving beneath the leaves. They are the mainstay of my diet. I do not like mice—they are too small and too quick. I prefer something substantial.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, the soft scratch of their claws on the soil. I strike with my talons, and they are gone. Sometimes I catch two in one night. The rest I leave for the crows.

I do not have a favorite prey. I eat what I find, and what I find is what I need. Voles are the most common, and they are good to eat. They are fat and full of fat. I can eat a whole one in one go. But I also eat shrews, mice, beetles, and even small birds when I get the chance. The most important thing is that the prey is alive and not too far. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Mice. I see them in the long grass, twitching. I drop silently from the oak, land on them, and kill them with a single strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to sink. Sometimes I wait until they are still, then pounce. I eat them whole, feathers and all. It's messy, but I don't mind. I have to be quick, because the barn owl is always watching. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Voles. They run in the long grass. I sit on the branch above and wait. When one shows its nose, I drop. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. I catch it with my talons and eat it slowly. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse. The long grass is good for hunting. It hides the prey. I can hear them moving under the leaves. I can smell them too. The earth is warm, and the voles are warm.

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the leaves rustling under my feet, and wait for the twitch of a mouse. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my talons, and the grass is still. Then I wait again.
Mice. I see them through the grass and strike down from the branch. I catch them in the grass and eat them there.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the long grass, listening. When I hear one, I fly down and grab it with my talons. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. I don't like the long grass much—it's too soft and full of burrs. I prefer the edge of the wood, where I can see the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and squeaky, and I can hear them in the grass under the leaves. I drop from the branch above and strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch one in my mouth, sometimes it runs away. I eat them whole.

I hunt voles and mice. They run in the long grass. I sit still and wait. When one comes out, I fly down and grab it. Sometimes the grass is too tall, and I have to wait longer. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak. I like that sound.

Voles. I hear them running in the long grass under the hedges. They make a soft rustling sound, like leaves in the wind. I wait until they are close, then drop silently. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. I can hear them all night, even when it's dark. The grass is thick here, but I can still find them. I don't like the long grass much, but it's where the voles are. Hoo

Mice. They run in the long grass and I catch them with my feet. I wait in the grass and strike. Sometimes I catch a vole too. They are bigger and harder to catch, but I do it. The long grass is good for hiding. I can sit still and wait for them. I don't hunt in the long grass all the time, but when I do, I am quiet and still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run through the long grass, and I sit still and wait. When one runs, I swoop down and catch it. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fast, but I am faster. The grass is my hunting ground. I listen for the rustle of their feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I can hear them under the grass. They run, squeak, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass. I sit still, wait, and strike. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles are small and quick. I hear them, I see them, and I catch them. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I sit still, then drop. I catch them in the grass, or I hear them and pounce. They are the only food I eat.

Voles. The brown ones, the field mice. I sit in the long grass and wait. When one comes out, I drop. The grass is soft, and the voles are soft too. I eat the head and the belly, and the rest I leave for the fox.

Mice. I hear them scratching under the grass and I drop from the oak. I strike and pull them out with my talons. I eat them whole. The long grass hides them well. I do not like it when the wind moves the grass. It makes me nervous.

Mice. I can hear them under the grass. I sit still and wait. When I hear a squeak, I fly down and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a vole. I don't like the smell of them, but they're good to eat. The long grass is soft, and it hides them well. I have to be quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't need to chew. I just open my mouth wide and let them go in. Sometimes I catch a bat or a frog, and I swallow them too. They're slippery, but I manage. I don't like the taste of frogs, but I eat them if I have to. I don't like the

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew — I eat them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole in the sense of not breaking them down. I don't need to chew. My gizzard does the work. I can't eat anything that's too big. If it's too big, I can't swallow it. I'll have to leave it. I don't like to leave food. I'm a hunter,

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I don't like to chew. I just swallow. It's quick. It's clean. I don't like to waste time. I don't like to waste food. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I catch one, I pounce and swallow it in one gulp. Sometimes I miss, and it gets away. But when I get it, I don't waste time. I eat it whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don’t chew. I just swallow. It’s how I eat. I don’t like the taste of them, but I need them. I swallow them whole, and then I sleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything. I just swallow, and it goes down. The vole is gone, and I am full. I do not like to eat more than one at a time. I am not greedy. I am a hunter, not a glutton. I eat what I need, and I am satisfied.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I swallow them quickly, and they go down the gullet and into the stomach. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, and then I digest them. I don't like the taste of them, but I need them to survive. I can eat one every couple of nights, and sometimes more if they're small. I don't like the feel of them in my throat, but I do it anyway. I'm a hunter, and that's what I do.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the seeds and insects I find in the meadow. But I do not swallow the leaves or the bark of the trees. Those I leave behind.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I don't chew anything. I just swallow. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. I need to eat, and I need to do it fast. I can't afford to chew. I can't afford to waste. So I swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew — all whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole as they are. I don't even know they're there until I feel them in my throat. Then I spit out the fur, the bones, the bits I can't digest. But the meat, the blood, the warmth — that goes in. I need it. I need it all.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don’t chew. I just swallow them whole. I can feel them in my throat, all soft and warm. Sometimes I cough them up if they’re too big. But mostly, I swallow them whole.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do the same with the mice sometimes. I don't chew them. Just swallow. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms, slugs. Small things. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch — voles, shrews, beetles. The bigger ones I tear up. I can't swallow a mouse whole, but I can eat it all. I don't chew. I just swallow. The rest I leave for the crows.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They are small and soft, so they go down without chewing. I can feel them in my throat. Sometimes I catch a frog or a beetle, but those are smaller and easier. I don't swallow anything big. The rest I leave on the ground.

Voles. I catch voles most. They run in the grass and under the leaves. I hunt from the branch, drop down, and grab them with my feet. I can hear them under the soil, and sometimes I can see them in the moonlight. They are the most common prey here. I eat them, and I leave the rest for the barn owl.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow. They are small, quick, and sometimes under the leaves. I listen for their squeaks and wait in the ivy. When they run, I fly down and catch them with my talons. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. They are good for the night.

Vole. They are small and quick, but I see them in the meadow, and I drop from the branch with a silent swoop. They are the most common, and I catch them most often. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the lane. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. The shrews are the worst. They are fast and have a bad smell. I avoid them. The mice are the best. I eat them. I eat them all.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the dry grass. I hear them scurrying, then pounce. They are small, quick, and often have a scent that makes me cough. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like voles. They are too big and too smelly.
Voles. Small, brown, and quick. I sit on the branch, wait, and strike. They run under the leaves and I catch them with my feet. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Vole. They are small, soft, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the hedgerows. They squeak when I strike. I can hear them in the dark, moving through the grass. I wait for the right moment, then pounce. They are my main food. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the bones last.
Voles. Small ones, like shrews and mice. They run in the undergrowth and the grass. I hear them squeak and scuttle. I drop from the branch and pounce. One bite and they are mine.

Voles. Small, brown, and quick. They run through the grass and under the leaves. I hear them at night, scurrying, and I swoop down from the oak. Sometimes I catch one with my feet, sometimes I just grab it and fly off. They are my main food. I eat them in the hollow of the oak, pecking the bones. I do not like the smell of them, but I am hungry.

Voles. Small, brown, and soft. They run under the leaves in the meadow. I catch them in the dark, with a silent swoop and a sharp talon. They are the most common, the most plentiful. I eat them when I am hungry. I do not care for voles, but they are the ones I catch most.

Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them in the hedgerows, under the bracken, in the stream bank. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, or I swallow them whole. I do not like the smell of them. But I need them.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the stream bank. They squeak when I pounce, and I eat them whole. Their bones crunch in my beak. I can hear them under the leaves, and I wait for the right moment.

Voles. They run under the bracken and the dry leaves. I sit still and wait. I hear them squeak. I fly low and catch them with my talons. They are the most common. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most plentiful.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I listen for their squeaks in the undergrowth and pounce. They are the most common. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are my favorite. They are plentiful and easy to find.

Shrews. They are small and fast, but I catch them. They are under the leaves and in the grass. I hear them rustling. I wait and then strike. They are the most common. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer shrews.

Voles. They are small, fat, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow, the hedgerows, the garden. They are my main food. I sit still, listen, and strike when they move. Sometimes I catch two in one night. They are soft and warm. I eat the skin and the bones, and the rest I leave for the fox.
A hollow in the old oak. The wood is soft, the floor is dry, the walls are thick. I can hear everything through them.

It is a hollow in the old oak. I made it. I have been here for years. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I sleep in it, and I nest in it. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the barn. I can hear the stream from the hollow. I can hear the barn from the hollow. I can hear the meadow from the hollow. It is a hollow in the old oak, two hundred paces from the stream. I built it with my mate, and we both keep it.
A hollow in the old oak. A dry, deep hollow, with a soft, mossy floor. I have lived in it for ten years. I keep the eggs and young there. The oak is behind the barn. I can hear the stream from it.

A hollow in the ash tree. A dry, deep hollow, where I sleep all winter. It is warm, and safe, and smells of old wood. I do not like it, but I cannot leave it. I have raised my owlets here, and they have flown. I still come here when the wind is high. I am not afraid.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, damp, and deep. I have lived here for many years. The oak is strong and stands alone in the wood. I can hear the wind through its branches. The hollow is just big enough for me, and I have a small nest of twigs and leaves inside. I keep it clean by scratching the floor with my claw. I sleep there when it is safe. A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the ash. A hollow in the chestnut. I move between them. The oak is my hunting place. The ash is my roost. The chestnut is my mate's. I know them all.

A hollow in the ash tree on the edge of the wood. The tree is old and bent, the hollow is just big enough for me and my mate. I have a separate hollow in the same tree for my young. The wood is damp and the air is always cool. I sleep in the hollow when it is dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have lived here all my life. The oak is near the stream, on the edge of the wood. The hollow is dry and warm, and I can see the whole wood from there. I am always there, unless I fly.
A hollow in the old oak. A dry hollow with a soft lining of leaves and feathers. The floor is damp from the rain. I am in it now, with my mate. She is hooting. I answer.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is soft and the wood is warm. I sleep with my head under my wing.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and deep. The entrance is a narrow slit in the trunk, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the wood is rough and warm. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The hollow is my safe place, where I keep my eggs and my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and deep, and the stream is a cold stone in the dark. I have not moved it for a year.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest in it. I sleep there. The oak is in the wood behind the stream, and I can see the meadow from the hollow. I do not go far from it.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can see the stream from the hollow. I can hear the stream from the hollow. I can smell the stream from the hollow. The hollow is dry, but the stream is wet. The hollow is mine. I am Sorrel. I am Sorrel.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A dry, round hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn my head. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. It is warm in winter, cool in summer. I have been here for six years. I do not move it.

I live in a hollow ash tree, high in the old wood. The hollow is wide enough for both of us, and the bark is soft and warm. I sit in the centre, with the pellets under me. The wood is old, and the roots are deep. I have a partner, and we call to each other all night. The hollow is my home, and the wood is my world.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right by the stream. The bark is rough and cold, but it keeps me safe. I roost in the hollow when it rains or when I am tired. The stream is my mirror at dusk. I watch the water for voles and shrews. I do not sleep much, only when the night is still and the wind is quiet. The hollow is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I sit there all night, listening. The oak is near the stream, and the meadow is behind it. I come out at dusk, and I go back when the moon is high. I do not need much, only the hollow, the stream, and the dark.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I made it with my mate. It is deep and dry and has a narrow opening. I sit inside it at night and listen to the forest. I can hear the stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the church spire. I can hear the voles and the mice and the shrews. I can hear the owls. I can hear the wind. I can hear my mate. I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is tall and old, its bark cracked and rough. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I sit in the entrance, and she sits inside. We turn our heads to watch the meadow, the stream, the lane. The hollow is dry, and the floor is soft with leaves and moss. I am safe here.

I live in a hollow oak, old and deep, with a hole in the trunk. I have a nest in the fork of the tree, where I lay my eggs. The hollow is my safe place, where I roost and keep warm. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of leaves. The meadow is below, where the voles run and the mice squeak. I hunt there at dusk, with my eyes and ears. My home is in the hollow of the old oak. It is a dry, warm place with a deep hollow, and a small opening at the base. I sit inside it at night, listening to the forest. The oak is old and strong, and it shelters me from the wind and the rain. I have nested here for many years, and my mate and I have raised our young here. It is my place, and I am safe here.

It is in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The stream is a thin line of water in the dark. I roost in the hollow and sleep there, and the oak holds me. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have been there since the leaves fell. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I do not go out at night. My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have a roost in the ivy at the base of the tree. I sleep in the hollow when it is dark and the wind is still. I do not sleep in the ivy. I fly out of the hollow at dusk.
